# Writing Functions in R {#sec-writing-functions} ::: {.callout-note title="Learning Objectives"} After completing this chapter, you will be able to: - Write your own R functions using proper syntax - Specify function arguments with default values - Return single or multiple values from functions - Use control flow (if/else, case_when) within functions - Understand lexical scoping and function environments - Apply functional programming principles with lapply and purrr - Iterate over single and multiple inputs efficiently - Choose between for loops and functional approaches ::: ## Why Write Your Own Functions? {#sec-why-functions} Throughout this book, we've used many functions: some from base R [@rproject2024] (like `mean()` and `sum()`), others from packages (like `dplyr::filter()` and `ggplot2::ggplot()`) [@wickham2019tidyverse]. But the real power of programming comes from writing your own functions. (@sec-writing-simple-functions gave a first taste; here we go further.) Functions allow you to **avoid repetition** by writing code once and using it many times. When you find yourself copying and pasting the same block of code with minor changes, that's a sign you should write a function. This also **reduces errors**—if you find a bug, you fix it in one place rather than tracking down every copy. Functions **improve readability** by letting you give meaningful names to complex operations; `calculate_gc_content(sequence)` is far clearer than the five lines of code it might contain. And functions make it easy to **share code** with colleagues or package your solutions for the broader community. In biosciences, you'll often need custom functions for domain-specific tasks: calculating enzyme kinetics parameters, normalizing gene expression data, computing population genetics statistics, or processing experimental replicates according to your lab's specific protocols. ## Basic Function Syntax {#sec-function-syntax} All R functions follow the same basic syntax: ```r function_name = function(ARGUMENTS) { OPERATIONS return(VALUE) } ``` Let's break this down: - **function_name**: A descriptive name for your function - **ARGUMENTS**: Input values the function accepts - **OPERATIONS**: What the function does - **return(VALUE)**: What the function gives back For short functions, you can write everything on one line: ```r my_short_func = function(x) x^2 ``` ::: {.callout-tip} Give your functions short, descriptive names that indicate what they do. `calculate_gc_content` is better than `func1` or `cgc`. ::: ## A Simple Example: GC Content Calculator {#sec-gc-example} Let's write a function that calculates the GC content of a DNA sequence --- the proportion of guanine (G) and cytosine (C) bases. (The same function is written in Python in @sec-py-functions.) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} gc_content = function(sequence) { # Convert to uppercase for consistency seq_upper = toupper(sequence) # Count G and C bases gc_count = str_count(seq_upper, "[GC]") # Calculate total length (excluding any non-ATGC characters) total_bases = str_count(seq_upper, "[ATGC]") # Return GC proportion gc_count / total_bases } ``` ::: Test it: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} gc_content("ATGCGATCGATCG") #> [1] 0.5384615 gc_content("atgcGATCgatcg") # Works with mixed case #> [1] 0.5384615 gc_content("AAAAAATTTTTT") # Low GC content #> [1] 0 gc_content("GGGGGGCCCCCC") # High GC content #> [1] 1 ``` ::: ### Specifying Return Values {#sec-specifying-return-values} In the example above, R automatically returned the last evaluated expression. However, it's good practice to use explicit `return()` statements, especially for complex functions: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} gc_content = function(sequence) { seq_upper = toupper(sequence) gc_count = str_count(seq_upper, "[GC]") total_bases = str_count(seq_upper, "[ATGC]") gc_proportion = gc_count / total_bases return(gc_proportion) # Explicit return } ``` ::: ### Returning Multiple Values {#sec-returning-multiple-values} What if we want to return more than one piece of information? Use a list or data frame: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} gc_content_detailed = function(sequence) { seq_upper = toupper(sequence) # Count each base a_count = str_count(seq_upper, "A") t_count = str_count(seq_upper, "T") g_count = str_count(seq_upper, "G") c_count = str_count(seq_upper, "C") total = a_count + t_count + g_count + c_count gc_prop = (g_count + c_count) / total # Return as a data frame result = tibble( sequence = sequence, length = total, A = a_count, T = t_count, G = g_count, C = c_count, gc_content = round(gc_prop, 4) ) return(result) } gc_content_detailed("ATGCGATCGATCGATCG") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|sequence | length| A| T| G| C| gc_content| |:-----------------|------:|--:|--:|--:|--:|----------:| |ATGCGATCGATCGATCG | 17| 4| 4| 5| 4| 0.5294|
::: ::: ### Default Argument Values {#sec-default-argument-values} You can specify default values for arguments. This is useful when most calls will use the same value: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} gc_content = function(sequence, digits = 4) { seq_upper = toupper(sequence) gc_count = str_count(seq_upper, "[GC]") total_bases = str_count(seq_upper, "[ATGC]") gc_proportion = gc_count / total_bases return(round(gc_proportion, digits)) } gc_content("ATGCGATCGATCG") # Uses default 4 digits #> [1] 0.5385 gc_content("ATGCGATCGATCG", 2) # Override to 2 digits #> [1] 0.54 ``` ::: ## Environments and Lexical Scoping {#sec-lexical-scoping} An important concept to understand is that functions operate in their own **environment**. Objects created inside a function don't appear in your global environment: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} test_function = function(x) { internal_var = x * 2 # This stays inside the function return(internal_var) } result = test_function(5) result #> [1] 10 # Try to access internal_var - it doesn't exist in the global environment # internal_var # Would produce an error ``` ::: This is called **lexical scoping**. R looks for objects in this order: 1. Inside the function 2. In the environment where the function was defined 3. In parent environments, up to the global environment ::: {.callout-important} Functions are "sandboxed" --- they don't pollute your global environment with intermediate variables. This makes code cleaner and reduces the risk of naming conflicts. ::: ## Control Flow in Functions {#sec-control-flow} ### Using if/else {#sec-using-if-else} Control flow allows your functions to behave differently based on conditions: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Calculate enzyme velocity using Michaelis-Menten kinetics enzyme_velocity = function(substrate, vmax, km, inhibitor = NULL, ki = NULL) { if (is.null(inhibitor)) { # No inhibitor: standard Michaelis-Menten velocity = (vmax * substrate) / (km + substrate) } else { # Competitive inhibition if (is.null(ki)) { stop("If inhibitor concentration is provided, ki must also be specified") } apparent_km = km * (1 + inhibitor / ki) velocity = (vmax * substrate) / (apparent_km + substrate) } return(velocity) } # Test without inhibitor enzyme_velocity(substrate = 10, vmax = 100, km = 5) #> [1] 66.66667 # Test with inhibitor enzyme_velocity(substrate = 10, vmax = 100, km = 5, inhibitor = 2, ki = 3) #> [1] 54.54545 ``` ::: ### Using case_when for Multiple Conditions {#sec-fn-case-when} When you have many conditions, nested `if/else` statements become hard to read. Use `dplyr::case_when()` instead: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Classify gene expression fold changes classify_expression = function(fold_change) { category = case_when( fold_change >= 2 ~ "strongly_upregulated", fold_change >= 1.5 ~ "upregulated", fold_change <= 0.5 ~ "strongly_downregulated", fold_change <= 0.67 ~ "downregulated", TRUE ~ "unchanged" ) return(category) } # Test with a vector of fold changes fold_changes = c(0.3, 0.6, 1.0, 1.6, 2.5) classify_expression(fold_changes) #> [1] "strongly_downregulated" "downregulated" "unchanged" #> [4] "upregulated" "strongly_upregulated" ``` ::: The equivalent `data.table::fcase()` function works similarly: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} classify_expression_dt = function(fold_change) { fcase( fold_change >= 2, "strongly_upregulated", fold_change >= 1.5, "upregulated", fold_change <= 0.5, "strongly_downregulated", fold_change <= 0.67, "downregulated", default = "unchanged" ) } classify_expression_dt(fold_changes) #> [1] "strongly_downregulated" "downregulated" "unchanged" #> [4] "upregulated" "strongly_upregulated" ``` ::: ## Iteration and Functional Programming {#sec-iteration} ### The Problem with for Loops {#sec-the-problem-with-for-loops} You'll often need to apply the same operation to many inputs. The traditional approach uses `for` loops (@sec-r-for-loops): ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Calculate GC content for multiple sequences sequences = c("ATGCGATCG", "GGGGCCCC", "AAAATTTT", "ATATATAT") # Using a for loop gc_results = NULL for (i in 1:length(sequences)) { gc_results[i] = gc_content(sequences[i]) } gc_results #> [1] 0.5556 1.0000 0.0000 0.0000 ``` ::: This works, but has several problems: 1. **Verbose**: Lots of boilerplate code 2. **Error-prone**: Easy to make off-by-one errors 3. **Pollutes environment**: The loop variable `i` persists after the loop 4. **Not R-like**: R is designed for vectorized operations ### Functional Programming with lapply {#sec-lapply} The **functional programming** approach treats iteration as applying a function across elements: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Much cleaner! gc_results = lapply(sequences, gc_content) gc_results #> [[1]] #> [1] 0.5556 #> #> [[2]] #> [1] 1 #> #> [[3]] #> [1] 0 #> #> [[4]] #> [1] 0 ``` ::: The result is a list. To get a vector instead: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} gc_results = sapply(sequences, gc_content) gc_results #> ATGCGATCG GGGGCCCC AAAATTTT ATATATAT #> 0.5556 1.0000 0.0000 0.0000 ``` ::: To combine results into a data frame, use our detailed function with `bind_rows()`: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} lapply(sequences, gc_content_detailed) %>% bind_rows() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|sequence | length| A| T| G| C| gc_content| |:---------|------:|--:|--:|--:|--:|----------:| |ATGCGATCG | 9| 2| 2| 3| 2| 0.5556| |GGGGCCCC | 8| 0| 0| 4| 4| 1.0000| |AAAATTTT | 8| 4| 4| 0| 0| 0.0000| |ATATATAT | 8| 4| 4| 0| 0| 0.0000|
::: ::: ### Using purrr for Iteration {#sec-purrr-map} The **purrr** package provides a consistent and powerful set of mapping functions (base R's `apply()` family, @sec-apply-family, plays the same role): ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # map() returns a list (like lapply) map(sequences, gc_content) #> [[1]] #> [1] 0.5556 #> #> [[2]] #> [1] 1 #> #> [[3]] #> [1] 0 #> #> [[4]] #> [1] 0 # map_dbl() returns a numeric vector map_dbl(sequences, gc_content) #> [1] 0.5556 1.0000 0.0000 0.0000 # map_df() returns a data frame map_df(sequences, gc_content_detailed) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|sequence | length| A| T| G| C| gc_content| |:---------|------:|--:|--:|--:|--:|----------:| |ATGCGATCG | 9| 2| 2| 3| 2| 0.5556| |GGGGCCCC | 8| 0| 0| 4| 4| 1.0000| |AAAATTTT | 8| 4| 4| 0| 0| 0.0000| |ATATATAT | 8| 4| 4| 0| 0| 0.0000|
::: ::: ### Creating and Reusing Named Functions {#sec-creating-and-reusing-named-functions} For complex analyses, separate the function definition from iteration: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Define a function for processing protein sequences analyze_protein = function(sequence) { seq_upper = toupper(sequence) length = nchar(seq_upper) # Count hydrophobic residues (simplified) hydrophobic = str_count(seq_upper, "[AILMFVPW]") # Count charged residues charged = str_count(seq_upper, "[DEKRH]") tibble( sequence = sequence, length = length, hydrophobic_pct = round(hydrophobic / length * 100, 1), charged_pct = round(charged / length * 100, 1) ) } # Some sample protein sequences proteins = c( "MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQLEERLGLIEVQAPILSRVGDGTQDNLSGAEKAVQVKVKALPDAQFEVVHSLAKWKRQQIAAALEHHHHHH", "MVLSPADKTNVKAAWGKVGAHAGEYGAEALERMFLSFPTTKTYFPHFDLSH", "GLSDGEWQQVLNVWGKVEADIAGHGQEVLIRLFTGHPETLEKFDKFKHLKTEAEMKASEDLKKHGTVVLTALGGILKKKGHHEAELKPLAQSHATKHKIPIKYLEFISDAIIHVLHSKHPGDFGADAQGAMTKALELFRNDIAAKYKELGFQG" ) # Apply to all proteins map_df(proteins, analyze_protein) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|sequence | length| hydrophobic_pct| charged_pct| |:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------:|---------------:|-----------:| |MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQLEERLGLIEVQAPILSRVGDGTQDNLSGAEKAVQVKVKALPDAQFEVVHSLAKWKRQQIAAALEHHHHHH | 92| 42.4| 32.6| |MVLSPADKTNVKAAWGKVGAHAGEYGAEALERMFLSFPTTKTYFPHFDLSH | 51| 47.1| 25.5| |GLSDGEWQQVLNVWGKVEADIAGHGQEVLIRLFTGHPETLEKFDKFKHLKTEAEMKASEDLKKHGTVVLTALGGILKKKGHHEAELKPLAQSHATKHKIPIKYLEFISDAIIHVLHSKHPGDFGADAQGAMTKALELFRNDIAAKYKELGFQG | 153| 41.2| 34.6|
::: ::: ## Iterating Over Multiple Inputs {#sec-multiple-inputs} Sometimes you need to iterate over multiple inputs simultaneously. ### Using pmap for Multiple Arguments {#sec-pmap} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Simulate growth curves with different parameters simulate_growth = function(time, k, n0, carrying_capacity) { # Logistic growth model n = carrying_capacity / (1 + ((carrying_capacity - n0) / n0) * exp(-k * time)) tibble( time = time, k = k, n0 = n0, K = carrying_capacity, population = round(n, 0) ) } # Parameters for different bacterial strains params = tibble( k = c(0.5, 0.8, 0.3), # Growth rates n0 = c(100, 50, 200), # Initial populations carrying_capacity = c(10000, 15000, 8000) # Carrying capacities ) # Run simulations for each strain at time = 10 pmap_df(params, ~simulate_growth(time = 10, k = ..1, n0 = ..2, carrying_capacity = ..3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| time| k| n0| K| population| |----:|---:|---:|-----:|----------:| | 10| 0.5| 100| 10000| 5999| | 10| 0.8| 50| 15000| 13633| | 10| 0.3| 200| 8000| 2720|
::: ::: ### Using a Data Frame of Inputs {#sec-using-a-data-frame-of-inputs} A cleaner approach for complex cases is to pass a data frame of input combinations (@fig-df-inputs shows the result): ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Create all parameter combinations simulation_params = expand.grid( time = seq(0, 20, by = 2), strain = c("wild_type", "mutant_A", "mutant_B") ) %>% as_tibble() %>% mutate( k = case_when( strain == "wild_type" ~ 0.5, strain == "mutant_A" ~ 0.8, strain == "mutant_B" ~ 0.3 ), n0 = 100, carrying_capacity = 10000 ) # Function that takes a row of parameters run_simulation = function(row_data) { simulate_growth( time = row_data$time, k = row_data$k, n0 = row_data$n0, carrying_capacity = row_data$carrying_capacity ) %>% mutate(strain = row_data$strain) } # Run all simulations results = map_df(1:nrow(simulation_params), function(i) { run_simulation(simulation_params[i, ]) }) # Plot the results ggplot(results, aes(x = time, y = population, color = strain)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point() + labs( title = "Bacterial Growth Curves", x = "Time (hours)", y = "Population Size", color = "Strain" ) + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Simulated bacterial growth curves for three strains, produced by mapping a function over a data frame of parameter combinations](15-writing-functions_files/figure-html/fig-df-inputs-1.png){#fig-df-inputs fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## A Worked Example: Normalizing Gene Counts {#sec-fn-worked-example} The examples so far have been small on purpose. Here is a function of the kind you will actually write, built up in the way functions get built in practice: first as a few lines that work once, then as something reusable. The raw read counts in the stickleback data (@sec-course-dataset) are not directly comparable between fish, because some libraries were sequenced more deeply than others. The usual first step is to scale each fish's counts to **counts per million** (CPM), dividing by that fish's total and multiplying by a million, and often to take a logarithm afterwards so that a handful of very highly expressed genes do not dominate every plot. Written once, for one column, that is a single line: `stickle$Gene1 / sum(stickle[, 5:604]) * 1e6`. Written for every gene it becomes a loop, and written for the next dataset it becomes a copy of the loop with the column numbers changed by hand, which is exactly the moment @sec-why-functions warned about. The function below does the job for any data frame whose gene columns can be named. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) normalize_cpm <- function(counts, gene_cols, log = TRUE, pseudocount = 1) { # counts: a data frame with one row per sample # gene_cols: a tidyselect specification of the count columns, e.g. starts_with("Gene") # log: if TRUE, return log2(CPM + pseudocount); if FALSE, return CPM # pseudocount: added before the log so that zero counts stay finite gene_mat <- counts |> select({{ gene_cols }}) |> as.matrix() if (!is.numeric(gene_mat)) stop("The selected gene columns must all be numeric.") if (any(gene_mat < 0, na.rm = TRUE)) stop("Counts cannot be negative.") library_size <- rowSums(gene_mat, na.rm = TRUE) cpm <- gene_mat / library_size * 1e6 if (log) cpm <- log2(cpm + pseudocount) counts |> select(-{{ gene_cols }}) |> bind_cols(as_tibble(cpm)) } ``` ::: Several of the chapter's ideas are at work in these fifteen lines. The arguments have **defaults** (@sec-default-argument-values), so the common call is short and the unusual one is still possible. The **input checks** at the top (@sec-fn-validate-inputs) fail immediately, with a message that says what went wrong, rather than producing a plausible-looking matrix of nonsense several steps later. The double-brace `{{ gene_cols }}` is the tidyverse's way of letting a function accept a column specification such as `starts_with("Gene")` and pass it on to `select()`; it is the one piece of syntax here that is specific to writing functions around dplyr, and it is worth recognizing because you will see it in other people's code. And the function returns a **data frame of the same shape it was given**, with the sample metadata untouched and the count columns replaced, so it drops straight into a pipeline. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} stickle <- read_tsv("../data/Stickle_RNAseq.tsv", show_col_types = FALSE) stickle_cpm <- normalize_cpm(stickle, starts_with("Gene")) stickle_cpm[1:4, 1:7] ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Individual |Genotype |Microbiota |Geno&Micro | Gene1| Gene2| Gene3| |:----------|:--------|:------------|:----------|--------:|--------:|--------:| |AC1 |A |conventional |convA | 6.372507| 6.280558| 8.508702| |AC2 |A |conventional |convA | 5.201244| 4.985373| 8.527971| |AC3 |A |conventional |convA | 5.775734| 5.609096| 7.049595| |AC4 |A |conventional |convA | 5.415360| 6.566381| 6.306388|
::: ```{.r .cell-code} # The raw counts and the normalized values tell different stories about library depth tibble(raw_total = rowSums(select(stickle, starts_with("Gene"))), cpm_total = rowSums(2^select(stickle_cpm, starts_with("Gene")) - 1)) |> summary() #> raw_total cpm_total #> Min. :125986 Min. :1e+06 #> 1st Qu.:190894 1st Qu.:1e+06 #> Median :204544 Median :1e+06 #> Mean :284009 Mean :1e+06 #> 3rd Qu.:371757 3rd Qu.:1e+06 #> Max. :582646 Max. :1e+06 ``` ::: After normalization every fish's counts sum to (almost exactly) one million, which is the point: differences between fish now reflect biology rather than how much sequencing each one received. Applying the same function to a second dataset, or with `log = FALSE`, or with a different pseudocount, is now a one-line change instead of a search-and-replace. ::: {.callout-note title="When to promote code into a function"} A useful rule of thumb is the second copy. The first time you write a block of code, write it inline and get it working. The moment you find yourself copying it, stop and turn it into a function, giving the things that differ between the copies names as arguments. Two copies are a smell; three are a bug waiting to happen, because you will fix one and forget the others. ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Testing a function you just wrote"} Check a new function on an input where you already know the answer before trusting it on real data. A two-row, three-gene data frame made with `tibble()` is enough to confirm by hand that the rows sum to a million and that `log = FALSE` returns raw CPM. Keep that check in your script as a comment or a tiny `stopifnot()`; it costs nothing and catches the day someone changes the function. ::: ## Best Practices for Writing Functions {#sec-function-best-practices} ### 1. Use Descriptive Names {#sec-fn-descriptive-names} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Good names calculate_gc_content() normalize_expression() fit_growth_curve() # Bad names func1() do_stuff() f() ``` ::: ### 2. Document Your Functions {#sec-fn-document} Add comments explaining what the function does, its arguments, and return value: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Calculate the melting temperature of a DNA primer # # Uses the Wallace rule for short oligonucleotides (<14 bp) # or the nearest-neighbor method for longer sequences # # Arguments: # sequence: DNA sequence (string of A, T, G, C) # method: "wallace" or "nearest_neighbor" # # Returns: # Melting temperature in degrees Celsius calculate_tm = function(sequence, method = "wallace") { seq_upper = toupper(sequence) length = nchar(seq_upper) a_count = str_count(seq_upper, "A") t_count = str_count(seq_upper, "T") g_count = str_count(seq_upper, "G") c_count = str_count(seq_upper, "C") if (method == "wallace" || length < 14) { # Wallace rule: Tm = 2(A+T) + 4(G+C) tm = 2 * (a_count + t_count) + 4 * (g_count + c_count) } else { # Simplified nearest-neighbor approximation tm = 64.9 + 41 * (g_count + c_count - 16.4) / length } return(tm) } calculate_tm("ATGCGATCGATCG") #> [1] 40 ``` ::: ### 3. Validate Inputs {#sec-fn-validate-inputs} Check that inputs are valid before processing: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} gc_content_safe = function(sequence) { # Check input type if (!is.character(sequence)) { stop("Sequence must be a character string") } # Check for valid DNA characters seq_upper = toupper(sequence) invalid_chars = str_remove_all(seq_upper, "[ATGCN]") if (nchar(invalid_chars) > 0) { warning(paste("Invalid characters removed:", invalid_chars)) } gc_count = str_count(seq_upper, "[GC]") total_bases = str_count(seq_upper, "[ATGC]") if (total_bases == 0) { stop("No valid DNA bases found in sequence") } return(gc_count / total_bases) } gc_content_safe("ATGCGATCG") # Works fine #> [1] 0.5555556 gc_content_safe("ATGCXYZGATCG") # Warning about invalid characters #> [1] 0.5555556 ``` ::: ### 4. Keep Functions Focused {#sec-fn-focused} Each function should do one thing well. Break complex operations into smaller functions: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Instead of one giant function, break it up: # Step 1: Clean the sequence clean_sequence = function(seq) { seq %>% toupper() %>% str_remove_all("[^ATGC]") } # Step 2: Calculate base composition base_composition = function(seq) { tibble( A = str_count(seq, "A"), T = str_count(seq, "T"), G = str_count(seq, "G"), C = str_count(seq, "C") ) } # Step 3: Derive statistics sequence_stats = function(composition) { total = sum(composition) composition %>% mutate( total = total, gc_content = (G + C) / total, at_content = (A + T) / total ) } # Combine them in a pipeline "atgcGATCgatcgNNNN" %>% clean_sequence() %>% base_composition() %>% sequence_stats() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| A| T| G| C| total| gc_content| at_content| |--:|--:|--:|--:|-----:|----------:|----------:| | 3| 3| 4| 3| 13| 0.5384615| 0.4615385|
::: ::: ## Summary {#sec-functions-summary} Writing functions is a fundamental programming skill that will dramatically improve your data analysis workflows: - **Basic syntax**: `function_name = function(args) { body; return(value) }` - **Return values**: Use explicit `return()` statements; return lists or data frames for multiple values - **Default arguments**: Provide sensible defaults for commonly-used parameter values - **Lexical scoping**: Functions operate in their own environment, keeping your global environment clean - **Control flow**: Use `if/else` and `case_when()` to handle different conditions - **Functional programming**: Prefer `lapply()`/`map()` over for loops for iteration - **Multiple inputs**: Use `pmap()` or data frame inputs for complex parameter combinations @sec-parallel-computing will show you how to run functions in parallel, catch errors gracefully (@sec-parallel-errors), and cache results for expensive computations (@sec-caching). ::: {.callout-tip} For quick reference on R function syntax and functional programming tools like `lapply()` and `purrr`, see @sec-appendix-r. ::: ## Additional Reading {#sec-fn-additional-reading .unnumbered} To deepen your understanding of functions and functional programming in R: - **[R for Data Science: Functions](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/functions)** [@wickham2023r] — Excellent introduction to writing functions - **[Advanced R: Functions](https://adv-r.hadley.nz/functions.html)** by Hadley Wickham — Deep dive into function mechanics - **[Advanced R: Functional Programming](https://adv-r.hadley.nz/fp.html)** — Closures, function factories, and more - **[R Packages](https://r-pkgs.org/)** by Wickham and Bryan — When you're ready to package your functions ## Exercises {#sec-fn-exercises .unnumbered} ::: {.callout-tip title="Practice Exercises"} **Exercise 1: Basic Function** Write a function called `count_codons()` that takes a DNA sequence and returns the number of complete codons (groups of 3 nucleotides). For example, "ATGCGA" has 2 complete codons. **Exercise 2: Function with Multiple Returns** Write a function `analyze_sequence()` that takes a DNA sequence and returns a data frame with: - The sequence length - GC content - Number of each base (A, T, G, C) - Whether it starts with a start codon (ATG) - Whether it ends with a stop codon (TAA, TAG, or TGA) **Exercise 3: Control Flow** Write a function `translate_codon()` that takes a three-letter codon and returns the corresponding amino acid (use a simplified table with just 5-10 codons). Include error handling for invalid inputs. **Exercise 4: Iteration** You have a vector of 10 DNA sequences. Use `map_df()` to apply your `analyze_sequence()` function from Exercise 2 to all of them and combine the results into a single data frame. **Exercise 5: Multiple Inputs** Write a function `dilution_series()` that takes an initial concentration and dilution factor, then returns a data frame showing the concentration at each step for a specified number of dilutions. Use `pmap()` to apply this to multiple starting conditions. **Exercise 6: Refactoring** Take the following for loop and rewrite it using functional programming: ```r results = c() for (i in 1:length(sequences)) { gc = gc_content(sequences[i]) if (gc > 0.5) { results = c(results, "high") } else { results = c(results, "low") } } ``` :::
